title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
lead: In a country village, Mrs Bennet hopes to marry her five daughters to men of fortune. A rich young man takes the great house nearby; his proud friend slights Elizabeth Bennet at a ball.

screens.label: Story so far
screens.text: Mrs Bennet hopes the rich newcomer Mr Bingley will marry one of her daughters. At the Meryton assembly he dances twice with Jane, while his friend Mr Darcy offends the room and slights Elizabeth. The families visit; Bingley's admiration for Jane grows, and Darcy begins to notice Elizabeth.

screens.label: What happens in full
paragraphs: Mrs Bennet tells her husband the news she has from Mrs Long: Netherfield Park has been let to Mr Bingley, a young man of large fortune from the north of England, who will move in before Michaelmas. He is single, with four or five thousand a year, and Mrs Bennet at once thinks of him as a husband for one of their five daughters.

She urges Mr Bennet to call on him as soon as he arrives, since the women cannot know him without that visit; Sir William and Lady Lucas mean to call for the same reason. Mr Bennet teases her. He suggests she and the girls go alone, offers to send a note consenting to any marriage, and puts in a word for Lizzy, whom he finds quicker than her sisters. Mrs Bennet protests that he always prefers Lizzy and has no pity for her nerves.

The narrator ends the chapter with a sketch of the pair. He is a mix of quick wit, sarcasm, reserve and whim that his wife has not understood in 23 years of marriage. She is slow, ill-informed and moody; the business of her life is to see her daughters married, and visiting and news are her comfort.

screens.label: What happens in full
paragraphs: Mr Bennet calls on Mr Bingley among the first of the neighbours, while still telling his wife he will not go, and keeps it from her until the evening after the visit.

At Longbourn, seeing Elizabeth trim a hat, he says he hopes Mr Bingley will like it. Mrs Bennet replies sourly that they cannot know his tastes, since they are not to visit. Elizabeth reminds her that Mrs Long has promised to introduce him at the assemblies, but Mrs Bennet distrusts Mrs Long, who has two nieces of her own. Annoyed, she scolds Kitty for coughing, and Kitty asks when the next ball is: in a fortnight.

Mr Bennet teases on. He offers to introduce Mr Bingley to Mrs Long himself, and asks Mary, the reader of great books, for her opinion; she has none ready. When Mrs Bennet declares she is sick of Mr Bingley, he says that is a pity, since he called on him that morning.

The family is astonished, as he intended. Mrs Bennet's annoyance turns to delight, and she claims she expected it all along. After he leaves the room she tells the girls what a good father they have and predicts that Bingley will dance with Lydia, who answers that she is the youngest but the tallest. The evening ends in guessing when he will return the visit and when to ask him to dinner.

questions.q: Why does the room turn against Darcy after first admiring him?
questions.a: His manners: he dances only with his own party, refuses introductions and seems above his company.

questions.q: How does Elizabeth react to the remark she overhears?
questions.a: She feels no warmth towards Darcy, but tells the story with spirit to her friends.

screens.label: What happens in full
paragraphs: Mrs Bennet and her daughters cannot get a description of Mr Bingley from Mr Bennet, so they rely on Lady Lucas: he is young, handsome and agreeable, and means to come to the next assembly with a large party. A few days later he returns Mr Bennet's visit and sits ten minutes in the library; from an upper window the daughters see only his blue coat and black horse. A dinner invitation is put off because he must go to London, and rumours grow about the size of his party.

At the Meryton assembly the party turns out to be five: Mr Bingley, his two sisters, Mr Hurst and Mr Darcy. Darcy is admired for his looks and his reported ten thousand a year, until his manner makes the room judge him proud and disagreeable. Bingley dances every dance, twice with Jane, and talks of giving a ball at Netherfield; Darcy dances only with Mrs Hurst and Miss Bingley.
While Elizabeth sits out two dances, she overhears Bingley urge Darcy to dance with her, and Darcy refuse, calling her only passable. She tells the story with spirit among her friends.

The family goes home pleased: Jane was admired, Mary was praised to Miss Bingley, and Kitty and Lydia never lacked partners. Mrs Bennet describes Bingley's partners to her husband, who begs her to stop, and then condemns Darcy's rudeness.

screens.label: What happens in full
paragraphs: Alone with Elizabeth after the assembly, Jane admits how much she admires Mr Bingley, and how flattered she was to be asked to dance a second time. Elizabeth teases her: Jane is always surprised by compliments and never sees a fault in anyone. Jane also thinks Bingley's sisters pleasing once one talks to them, and expects Miss Bingley, who will keep house for her brother, to be a charming neighbour. Elizabeth is not convinced.

The narrator sides with her. The sisters are fine, well-educated ladies with a fortune of £20,000, but proud and conceited, and readier to remember their good family in the north of England than that its money came from trade. Bingley inherited nearly £100,000 from his father, who meant to buy an estate; Bingley means to as well, but may stay at Netherfield, which he took after half an hour's look.

His friendship with Darcy is steady despite their opposite characters. Bingley is easy and open, and trusts Darcy's judgment; Darcy is cleverer, but haughty and reserved, and gives offence where Bingley is liked. Their views of the assembly differ in the same way: Bingley found everyone pleasant and Jane beautiful beyond compare; Darcy found little beauty and no fashion, and Jane pretty but too ready to smile. The sisters call Jane a sweet girl, and Bingley feels free to think of her as he likes.

screens.label: What happens in full
paragraphs: The Lucases live near Longbourn at Lucas Lodge. Sir William once traded in Meryton and was knighted after an address to the king as mayor; he then left business and the town, and now spends his time being civil to everyone. Lady Lucas is a kind woman and a good neighbour to Mrs Bennet. Their eldest daughter, Charlotte, about 27, is Elizabeth's close friend.

The morning after the assembly the Lucas daughters come to Longbourn to talk it over. Mrs Bennet notes that Charlotte was Bingley's first partner, but Charlotte says he liked his second better, and repeats what she overheard: asked which woman in the room was the prettiest, Bingley named the eldest Miss Bennet. Charlotte teases Elizabeth about Darcy's remark.

Mrs Bennet passes on Mrs Long's complaint that Darcy sat beside her for half an hour without a word; Jane says Miss Bingley told her he talks freely only among close friends. Charlotte excuses his pride, given his family and fortune. Elizabeth answers that his pride would be easy to forgive had he not wounded hers, and promises her mother never to dance with him. Mary lectures on the difference between pride and vanity, and a young Lucas boy says that if he were as rich as Darcy he would keep foxhounds and drink a bottle of wine a day.

screens.label: What happens in full
paragraphs: The Longbourn and Netherfield ladies exchange visits. Mrs Hurst and Miss Bingley warm to Jane, though they find Mrs Bennet intolerable and the younger girls not worth speaking to, and Elizabeth still sees their scorn for others. Bingley plainly admires Jane, and Elizabeth sees Jane falling in love, though Jane's calm manner hides it from the world.

Elizabeth tells Charlotte, who argues that Jane should show Bingley more feeling, not less, or she may lose him, and that a happy marriage is a matter of luck anyway. Elizabeth replies that Jane is not acting by design and has known him only a fortnight, and that Charlotte would never act on such a view herself.

Meanwhile Darcy, who first found Elizabeth barely pretty, is struck by her dark, intelligent eyes and her easy, playful manner, and begins to listen to her conversations. At a large party at Sir William Lucas's, Elizabeth notices this and, dared by Charlotte, teases him; then she plays and sings, and Mary takes over at the instrument while the younger girls dance with some officers.

Sir William, failing to draw Darcy into talk about dancing, presents Elizabeth to him as a partner; Darcy asks her to dance and she refuses. When Miss Bingley assumes he is despising the company, Darcy says he is thinking of Miss Elizabeth Bennet's fine eyes, and Miss Bingley teases him about marriage and a mother-in-law at Pemberley.
